summary: Mars Storm Crew is a browser-based game that lets children aged 7-12 manage a Mars outpost through the 2018 global dust storm that ended NASA’s Opportunity rover mission. In this project, water can be allocated either for drinking or for radiation shielding, forcing players to decide how to use a limited resource. When radiation levels rise, children must choose whether to contact Earth and wait through the Mars-Earth communication delay or take immediate action by seeking shelter. Importantly, a What if? replay feature lets players change one decision and compare two possible futures without penalty, encouraging experimentation and learning from consequences. The game is grounded in NASA open data: JPL Horizons for signal delay, Opportunity for dust, Curiosity’s RAD for the September 2017 solar event, and DONKI for space weather. Every news item is labeled Real Data, Based on a Real Event, Scenario, or Game Number, so children can distinguish real scientific information from simulated events. A mission code also allows an entire classroom to experience the same storm and compare their decisions. Mission reports use plain code, with no AI involved. Accessible directly through a browser link in both English and Vietnamese, Mars Storm Crew helps the next generation understand that every choice in space comes with a cost, take responsibility for their decisions, and develop curiosity about Mars, a planet that may one day become humanity’s second home.
details:
🎮 How It Works:

  • The Commander picks a face and types a nickname (kept only in this browser).
  • The game runs 30 sols, from 28 May to 26 June 2018. Sol 14 is 10 June 2018, the day of the Opportunity dust-opacity reading.
  • At 7 key sols, a news message with a source label appears, and the child picks a card that shows the gain and the loss.
  • Water Wall: the same water can be drunk or used as a radiation wall.
  • Ask Earth or decide now: the delay clock uses the real one-way Earth-Mars light time for that day (about 4 to 5 minutes in June 2018).
  • Real data cards: after sol 14, the child learns that dust blocks sunlight but not cosmic radiation; after sol 17, the child reads what Curiosity really measured (NASA OSDR RadLab).
  • A mission code sets the luck of the run: real storm or false alarm, second storm, misleading meter clue.
  • At the end: a mission report (success or rescue, not fail, just learning by mistake), the What if? replay, and a certificate PNG drawn in the browser. Nothing is uploaded, and the certificate says it is not an official NASA document.

🛠️ Technology Used:

  • TypeScript + React web app (Vite), deployed on Vercel. No backend, no account, no tracking.
  • The engine is a pure simulation that always gives the same run for the same input, so What if? re-runs it with one choice changed, and a class can replay the same storm.
  • Data files hold the Earth-Mars light time (JPL Horizons) and the dust haze curve.
  • NASA DONKI (ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI): radiation storms, strong M/X flares, and WSA-Enlil CMEs forecast to reach Mars over the last 30 days, fetched live. If NASA cannot be reached, the game uses the last saved answer, then a snapshot bundled at build time.
  • The mission report has no AI inside: it replays the simulation with every other option at each decision and compares the results.
  • Sounds are synthesized in the browser, so there are no audio files.
  • Font: Be Vietnam Pro (SIL OFL 1.1).
  • Automated tests check the game balance and text strings.

⭐ Key Features:

  • Water Wall: drink it or wall it
  • Real Earth-Mars signal delay
  • Mission codes: replay the same storm
  • What if? Replay and mission report
  • Four source labels on every news item
  • English and Vietnamese
  • Add to Home Screen on iPhone (full screen, landscape)
  • Certificate PNG made in the browser, nothing uploaded

💡 How Is It Creative?

  • One liter of water, two jobs: the trade-off is a picture children can see, not a number.
  • The story starts from a real, dated event: the 2018 storm that ended Opportunity.
  • Two different dangers, dust (takes power) and solar storms (bring radiation), are separated instead of mixed up.
  • Every run differs by mission code, and the mission report shows which choice was best, with no AI.

🧭 Factors We Considered:

  • Honesty: every news item is labeled, and only data we really have is called real. The dust curve is a game curve, and dust (Opportunity) and radiation (Curiosity) come from two different rovers, so the station is imagined.
  • Children’s safety and privacy: no account, no tracking, nickname stays in the browser, no AI talks to the child.
  • Accessibility: short messages, English and Vietnamese, works on a phone.
  • Reliability: DONKI has a saved fallback, so the game works if NASA cannot be reached.
  • Licensing: art packs are used within their licenses, so raw files are not in the public repository.
🎯 Benefits & Goals:

Today

  • Help children see that every mission resource is a trade-off.
  • Let them learn by replaying without penalty.
  • Show clearly what is real NASA data and what is a game number.
  • Give teachers and parents a free activity for a class or at home.
  • Reach children worldwide with English as the common language, and give Vietnamese children a full game in their mother tongue.

Vision

  • More languages: all text is kept in separate language strings, so new languages can be added without rebuilding the game.
  • Beyond Mars: the same trade-off engine and labeled-data approach can be extended to a lunar outpost, using lunar data such as Artemis mission data.
